openers.title: Shark on Main Street?
openers.prompt: Picture this photo, posted during a storm: a shark fin cuts through brown floodwater on Main Street in Cedar Bend, right past a stop sign. The caption says "THIS IS HAPPENING NOW. Share before they delete it!" What do you notice, what do you wonder, and what would you check before you believed it?
openers.teacher: Read the description twice, then give 60 seconds of silent think time before partners share one notice and one wonder. Ask: "Would zooming in on the photo settle it, or do you need to check something outside the photo?"
openers.answer: You cannot tell from the image alone. Old photos get reused, edits are easy, and AI can generate a scene like this in seconds. The strongest move is to leave the post and look for the source and for local news coverage of the storm.
openers.lookFor: Students name at least one check outside the image, such as who first posted it or whether local news reported it, instead of only hunting for visual glitches.
openers.next: Next, students test whether visual clues or source checks catch more fakes.

openers.title: The Lake That Isn't There
openers.prompt: A student asked a chatbot for help with a geography project. It answered: "Lake Pembrook is the deepest lake in Texas, at 912 feet. It was formed by a meteor about 10,000 years ago." Fact or fake?
openers.teacher: Students show one finger for Fact, two for Fake, three for Can't tell yet. Call on one student from each group to explain, then ask: "What would you do next if this showed up in your notes?"
openers.answer: Fake. Lake Pembrook is invented for this opener, and so are the depth and the meteor story. A chatbot predicts likely-sounding words, so it can state made-up details with total confidence. "Can't tell yet" is a smart first answer; the fix is to check an atlas or a trusted source before you use it.
openers.lookFor: Students explain that sounding confident or specific is not the same as being true, and they name a source they would check.
openers.next: Later, students build a paper word-guessing machine and watch it invent a fact on its own.

openers.title: Shortcut or Study Help?
openers.prompt: Sort these five AI uses into "builds my learning" or "replaces my learning": 1) asking AI to quiz me on vocabulary, 2) pasting in my essay question and turning in the answer, 3) asking AI to explain fractions a different way, 4) having AI write my reading log, 5) asking AI what I might have missed in my science notes.
openers.teacher: Students jot the numbers under two or three headings on a whiteboard, then compare with a partner. Ask: "Pick one that depends. What would make it build learning instead of replace it?"
openers.answer: Uses 1, 3, and 5 keep you doing the thinking, so they usually build learning. Uses 2 and 4 hand the thinking to the tool. Any of them can shift: even a quiz stops helping if you just copy answers, which is why your teacher's rules and your honesty both matter.
openers.lookFor: Students give a reason tied to who is doing the thinking, not just whether AI was used.
openers.next: Students will turn these ideas into a personal AI study contract and honest-use log.

openers.title: Free Gems, Just Log In
openers.prompt: A message pops up in your game chat from "Mod_Zyra": "Congrats! You won 5,000 free gems for being a top player. Log in at gemdrop-rewards.co in the next 10 minutes or they expire." What do you do?
openers.teacher: Students move to three corners of the room, one for each option. Each corner names the clue that decided it for them. Ask: "If this message had zero spelling mistakes, would that make it safe?"
openers.answer: Treat it as a scam. The countdown, the prize you never entered for, and a login link outside the game are the real clues. Perfect spelling proves nothing because AI can polish scam messages. If you want to check, open the game yourself, never through the link, and tell a trusted adult.
openers.lookFor: Students point to pressure, the unexpected prize, or the outside login link rather than spelling as their reason.
openers.next: Teams will sort a full stack of texts, emails, and game messages into safe, scam, or check-another-way.

openers.title: Location: Always, Sometimes, Never?
openers.prompt: Would you rather share your live location with your friends all the time so it is easy to meet up, or keep it off and text people where you are when you need to? Either way, who else might be able to see where you go?
options: Share with friends all the time
Keep it off and text instead
openers.teacher: Students stand on one side of the room or the other, then talk with someone from the opposite side for one minute. Ask: "Is there a middle choice, like sharing only with family or only during a trip?"
openers.answer: There is no single right answer. Sharing is convenient and can help family keep you safe, but a trail of locations can reveal your home, school, and routine to more people than you meant. Many apps let you share with a short list or for a set time.
openers.lookFor: Students name a middle option, such as sharing with fewer people or for a limited time, and say who they would trust with their location.
openers.next: Students will map a fictional teen's Saturday from location pings and write their own settings checkup.

openers.title: Headline Meets Lede
openers.prompt: Headline: "HOMEWORK BANNED IN FERNWOOD SCHOOLS!" First sentence of the article: "A Fernwood district committee will spend the next year studying how much homework students get and may suggest changes." Does the headline match the story?
openers.teacher: Students hold up one, two, or three fingers. Partners then rewrite the headline in eight words or fewer so it matches the lede. Ask: "Why would someone write the first headline?"
openers.answer: It stretches it, almost to a contradiction. Nothing is banned; a committee is only studying the question. Dramatic headlines get more clicks and shares, which is why reading past the headline matters.
openers.lookFor: Rewritten headlines keep the real news (a committee is studying homework) and drop the claim that anything was banned.
openers.next: Later, students write their own future headlines and ledes and fact-check each other for clickbait.

openers.title: Draw the Feed's Rule
openers.prompt: Nico watched one skateboarding video all the way to the end. Now his feed is almost all skateboarding. Draw the rule the app might be following as a flowchart or an "IF ... THEN ..." sentence.
openers.teacher: Students sketch on scrap paper or whiteboards for three minutes, then compare with a partner. Ask: "What would Nico have to do to break the pattern, and what might he never see now?"
openers.answer: A simple version: IF a person watches a video to the end, THEN show more videos like it. Real feeds use many signals, but the idea is the same: the app predicts what will keep you watching, which can narrow what you see.
openers.lookFor: Drawings show an input (what Nico did) leading to an output (what the feed shows next), and students suggest at least one way to widen the feed.
openers.next: Students will play the card-based Feed Game and watch a feed shrink by hand.

openers.title: Who Wrote the Script?
openers.prompt: Your group is making a two-minute video about a problem at school. One teammate says, "Let's just have AI write the whole script. It'll be done in a minute." Another says that feels like cheating. How should your team decide?
openers.teacher: Partners talk for three minutes, then each pair shares one rule their team would agree on. Ask: "Which parts of this project should stay your team's own ideas?"
openers.answer: Strong answers split the job: the team picks the problem and the message, AI might help brainstorm or give feedback if the teacher allows it, and the team checks and rewrites anything it keeps and says how AI helped.
openers.lookFor: Pairs propose a team agreement that names what AI may and may not do and how the team will be honest about it.
openers.next: Teams will use the design process on a real community problem and keep a record of what AI suggested and what they rejected.

openers.title: Picture a Scientist
openers.prompt: A teacher asked an image generator for "a scientist at work" four times. Every picture showed an older man with white hair and a lab coat, standing in a lab. What do you notice? Who is missing?
openers.teacher: Students list who is missing on a whiteboard (for example, women, young scientists, people who work outdoors or with computers), then pairs rewrite the prompt to get a fuller picture. Ask: "Where might the tool have learned this pattern?"
openers.answer: Image tools learn from huge piles of existing pictures and captions, so they can repeat old stereotypes. Scientists are all kinds of people doing all kinds of work. A more specific prompt can help, but noticing the pattern is the first step.
openers.lookFor: Students name specific missing groups or kinds of scientific work and write a prompt that includes them.
openers.next: Students will read six mock AI outputs through different perspectives and rewrite prompts to fix the bias.

openers.title: Rewrite the Roast
openers.prompt: A classmate posts their project slideshow in the class forum. Someone comments: "lol this is so boring, did a 3rd grader make this?" Rewrite the comment so it is honest, kind, and actually helpful.
openers.teacher: Students write for two minutes, then swap with a partner who checks for one specific suggestion. Ask: "What makes feedback useful instead of just nice or just mean?"
openers.answer: A helpful rewrite names something that works, one specific change, and a reason, such as "Your topic is interesting. Maybe add a photo on slide 3 so the example stands out."
openers.lookFor: Rewrites include at least one specific, doable suggestion and no insults or sarcasm.
openers.next: Use the same pattern the next time students give feedback on each other's work, online or on paper.

openers.title: One Screen Goal
openers.prompt: Think about yesterday. When did a screen help you, and when did it take time you wanted for something else? Write one small, realistic screen goal for this week and how you will know you met it.
openers.teacher: Students write privately for three minutes; share only if they choose. Ask volunteers: "What makes a goal realistic instead of too big?"
openers.lookFor: Goals are specific and checkable, such as "phone charges outside my room on school nights," not "use screens less."
openers.next: Students check their goal on Friday with a quick thumbs up, sideways, or down and adjust it for next week.

openers.title: Stand If You Check
openers.prompt: Stand up if the statement is true for you, then sit back down. 1) I have believed something online that turned out to be false. 2) I have checked a second source before sharing. 3) I have used an AI answer without checking it. 4) I know one habit I want to get better at.
openers.teacher: Read each statement and pause for students to stand. No one explains unless they volunteer. Finish by asking students to whisper to a partner the one checking habit they want to practice.
openers.lookFor: Students name a specific habit to improve, such as checking a second source or asking where an AI answer came from.
openers.next: Revisit the same statements in a month and notice what changed.

openers.title: Prompt Glow-Up
openers.prompt: Here is a weak prompt: "Tell me about volcanoes." With a partner, rewrite it so an AI would help you study for Friday's quiz on how volcanoes form, without just doing the work for you.
openers.teacher: Pairs rewrite the prompt for three minutes and share a few. Then you type the original and one student prompt into a district-approved chatbot on the projector (students do not use their own accounts). Ask: "Which answer helps you learn, and what would you still need to check?"
openers.answer: Stronger prompts say who you are, what you need, and how you want help, for example: "I'm in 7th grade. Quiz me with five questions about how volcanoes form and explain any I get wrong." Even a good answer still needs checking against your notes or textbook.
openers.lookFor: Rewritten prompts include the grade level, the specific topic, and a request that keeps the student thinking, such as a quiz or an explanation.
openers.next: Students try the same prompt pattern the next time the class uses an approved AI tool.

openers.title: The Landslide Chart
openers.prompt: Picture a bar chart titled "TACOS WIN BY A LANDSLIDE!" The taco bar towers over the pizza bar. But look closely at the side: the numbers start at 48, not 0. Tacos got 52 votes and pizza got 49. Is "landslide" fair?
openers.teacher: Students vote with fingers, then sketch the same chart with the axis starting at 0. Ask: "Why might someone start the axis at 48?"
openers.answer: Misleading. The numbers in this mock chart are close (52 to 49), but starting the axis at 48 makes the gap look huge. Always check where the axis starts before you trust how big a difference looks.
openers.lookFor: Redrawn charts start at 0 and show two bars of nearly the same height.
openers.next: Students will build an honest chart from a lunch survey and catch charts that mislead.

openers.title: Remix It Right
openers.prompt: Sort each remix: 1) using a song you found online as background music in a video you post publicly, 2) using a photo marked with a Creative Commons license and crediting the creator, 3) drawing your own version of a cartoon character for your notebook, 4) posting an AI-made image as if you drew it.
openers.teacher: Students sort the numbers on a whiteboard and compare in groups of three. Ask: "What changes when you post something publicly instead of keeping it for yourself?"
openers.answer: 1 needs permission or music you are allowed to use. 2 is okay because the license allows it and you gave credit. 3 is usually fine for personal practice. 4 is not okay; be honest that AI made it.
openers.lookFor: Students connect their choice to credit, permission, or honesty about AI, and notice that sharing publicly raises the stakes.
openers.next: Students will sort more remix decisions and write credit lines that include notes about AI help.
